extracted.intended_audience: researchers and grant applicants (life sciences and engineering); investigators preparing responses and resubmissions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice for researchers on how to interpret peer review feedback on grant proposals and craft constructive, proportionate responses and resubmissions to improve funding chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow funding agency instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Always read the instructions for grant preparation offered up by the funding agency and do everything they ask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and panels use instructions to triage proposals; failing to follow directions is a common reason for elimination. Examples of instruction failures include inappropriate font size, inappropriate page margins, poor formatting, inattention to word length restrictions, and incompleteness. If the author cannot follow simple instructions, reviewers view them as untrustworthy stewards of funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and submission compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere strictly to formatting, page limits, fonts, margins, and other submission requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting errors make a proposal an easy target for early elimination. Ensure correct font size, margins, page/word limits, and that no unrelated copy-paste text remains. Double-check the funder's specific technical requirements before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of hypotheses, aims, and supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must present clear hypotheses, well-defined aims, and appropriate supporting data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common defects in rejected proposals include unclear hypotheses, no supporting data, and unclear aims. Make hypotheses explicit, include preliminary or supporting data where appropriate, and ensure aims are understandable and logically connected to the hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrated innovation and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must demonstrate significance (an important, translational problem) and innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of significance or lack of innovation are described as 'fatal flaws.' Do background research to frame the problem's importance and emphasize novel aspects. If the proposed problem has little translational value or is unimportant, pivot to a more significant problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and feasibility (avoid overambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the proposed work to realistic time, resources, and investigator experience; avoid overambitious plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators frequently propose more than can be accomplished. Consult experienced scientists to assess whether the work is feasible with the available time and budget; scale back aims if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address investigator experience gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: If the team lacks experience in the proposed field, remedy this by collaborating or adjusting scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of experience can kill a proposal. Solutions include adding collaborators with relevant expertise, or targeting smaller grants that fund high-risk/high-reward work or exploratory projects in a new direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion management when responding
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove your emotions—do not respond while upset; take a break and clear your head before crafting responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection often provokes sadness, frustration, and anger. Step away from reviews for a few days, talk with colleagues, then return to objectively plan how to repair the proposal. Emotional distance improves judgement on how to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a two-column critique-response document
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide feedback into two columns: Column A lists all negative comments (combine duplicates); Column B lists how you intend to respond to those comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method helps quantify the nature and extent of criticisms, order your thoughts, and plan responses. You can also assign scores to comments to reveal which criticisms are most significant or common across reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret reviewer comment characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the style and length of reviewers' comments to infer how they reviewed the proposal and tailor responses accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, terse negative comments often indicate a reviewer who didn't read closely—respond by referencing areas they may have missed. Extensive, detailed criticisms usually indicate an engaged reviewer providing constructive feedback; treat these as opportunities for substantial improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to identify reviewers (cautiously)
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, try to infer reviewers' identities (e.g., by checking NIH reviewer lists) to better understand their perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a funder publishes reviewer names, use that to make educated guesses about who reviewed you and reference their work in your response where appropriate. Do not address or name reviewers directly in the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully consider and prioritize all criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume most reviewers aim to be constructive; critically evaluate each comment and decide how to address it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a small percentage of reviewers have an 'axe to grind.' Options for dealing with criticisms include: (a) paying deference in responses to disarm reviewers, (b) arguing the logic where you are the expert—sometimes reviewers will relent, or (c) ignoring minor/unwarranted critiques. Choose strategies strategically and document rationale in your response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand root causes before resubmitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Before resubmitting, take time to truly understand why the proposal was rejected and seek external assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk with experienced and successful grant writers to get an independent assessment. Your proposal may have fatal flaws (significance, innovation, scope, experience). Fix root causes rather than only addressing surface comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the right funding agency and mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure alignment between your proposal and the funder's priorities and mechanisms; repeated rejections may indicate a mismatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you keep being rejected, you might be applying to the wrong funding agency. Reassess funder priorities and consider alternative agencies or smaller mechanisms better suited to your project's stage and risk profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and use of expert advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful grant writing is a journey requiring solid preparation, expert feedback, and persistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect many rejections; learn from reviews, persistently improve proposals, seek mentorship and peer feedback, and iterate. Use available resources (webinars, curated funding opportunity platforms, personalized scouting reports) to build a strategic funding roadmap.
